name: Mungpoo
tagline: Tagore's hill retreat among the cinchona plantations
meta_description: Plan Mungpoo on a budget: Tagore's house at Rabindra Bhavan, the cinchona plantations, quiet homestays, how to reach and 2026 costs.
summary: Mungpoo is a small hill settlement at about 1,150 m, roughly 35 km from Darjeeling, built around the government cinchona plantation. Rabindranath Tagore stayed here at the house of Maitreyi Devi on visits between 1938 and 1940, and the house is now a museum, Rabindra Bhavan. Visit for half a day or stay a quiet night.
intro: Mungpoo is a plantation village rather than a tourist town. Its slopes are covered not with tea but with cinchona, the tree whose bark gives quinine, planted here by the colonial government in the nineteenth century and still managed by the West Bengal government. The settlement has staff quarters, a small bazaar, schools and the old factory buildings, with views down towards the Teesta valley. Most visitors come for one house.

That house belonged to the family of Maitreyi Devi, the Bengali writer, whose husband Dr Manmohan Sen worked as a chemist at the quinine factory. Rabindranath Tagore visited them here four times between 1938 and 1940, in the last years of his life, and wrote and read in the house. It is now Rabindra Bhavan, a small museum with his furniture, photographs and some of his paintings and letters. For many Bengali visitors, Mungpoo is a pilgrimage.

Mungpoo is cheap and quiet. There is little to buy and no nightlife, and the main costs are the car and a simple homestay or lodge if you stay over. It pairs naturally with Sittong's orange orchards and Kurseong's tea gardens, all within an hour or so. The roads are narrow and steep, and the monsoon months bring landslides, so come between October and May and check current status before you travel.

story.title: Tagore's last hill-station summers
paras: Maitreyi Devi, born in 1914, was the daughter of the philosopher Surendranath Dasgupta and had known Rabindranath Tagore since childhood. After her marriage to Dr Manmohan Sen, a chemist at the government quinine factory in Mungpoo, she invited the ageing poet to stay. Tagore came four times between 1938 and 1940. He worked, wrote and talked with his hosts in the quiet house on the hill, away from Santiniketan and Calcutta.

Maitreyi Devi later recorded those visits and conversations in her Bengali book Mangpute Rabindranath. She went on to write Na Hanyate, her reply to Mircea Eliade's novel about their youthful relationship in Calcutta, which won the Sahitya Akademi Award. The Mungpoo house was later turned into a museum, Rabindra Bhavan, with Tagore's belongings and pictures. Each year on his birth anniversary, local people and visitors gather there for songs and readings.

did_you_know: Rabindranath Tagore stayed at Maitreyi Devi's house in Mungpoo on four visits between 1938 and 1940.
Maitreyi Devi's novel Na Hanyate, written as a reply to Mircea Eliade's Bengal Nights, won the Sahitya Akademi Award.
The hills around Mungpoo are planted with cinchona, the tree whose bark is the source of the anti-malaria drug quinine.

highlights.title: Rabindra Bhavan, Tagore's Mungpoo house
highlights.text: The house where Tagore stayed as Maitreyi Devi's guest is now a small museum. See the room he used, his chair and desk, photographs, letters and reproductions of his paintings. It takes under an hour, and the caretakers are often happy to talk about the poet's visits.

highlights.title: Cinchona plantations
highlights.text: The slopes around Mungpoo are planted with cinchona, grown for quinine since the nineteenth century. Drive or walk the plantation roads to see the slender trees and the old factory buildings. It is one of the few places in India where this colonial-era crop still covers whole hillsides.

highlights.title: Tagore's birth anniversary
highlights.text: Every year on 25 Baishakh, which falls in early May, Rabindra Bhavan hosts songs, recitations and gatherings in Tagore's memory. Local schools and visitors from Bengal take part. If you can time your visit for it, Mungpoo feels very different from a quiet weekday.

highlights.title: Views towards the Teesta valley
highlights.text: Mungpoo stands on a slope above the Teesta valley, and the roads around it open onto wide views of forested ridges and the river country below. Morning light is best. On the clearest winter days, snow peaks show on the northern horizon.

highlights.title: An easy pairing with Sittong
highlights.text: Mungpoo and Sittong are close neighbours. Visit Rabindra Bhavan in the morning, drive on through the cinchona slopes, and spend the night in a Sittong homestay among orange orchards. In winter, the two make one of the quietest short trips in the Darjeeling hills.

how_to_reach.text: A few shared jeeps link Mungpoo with Darjeeling and with Siliguri via the Teesta road, usually once or twice a day, ₹100–200 a seat, indicative 2026. Timings change, so ask at the Darjeeling motor stand or your hotel the day before.

A reserved car from Darjeeling costs about ₹2,500–3,500 for a day trip, and from NJP or Bagdogra about ₹3,000–4,500 one way, indicative 2026. Drivers often combine Mungpoo with Sittong or Kurseong. Roads are narrow and winding; check current status before you travel in wet weather.

Bagdogra (IXB) is the nearest airport, about 65 km away, and NJP the nearest big station. The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway does not reach Mungpoo; the closest toy-train stations are Kurseong and Ghum, each about 1–1.5 hours away by road.

where_to_stay: Mungpoo has very few places to stay: a handful of small homestays and simple lodges, mostly with shared meals, at roughly ₹1,200–2,500 per person per day with food, indicative 2026. Most visitors come on a day trip or stay nearby. Sittong's orchard homestays are close and better set up for guests. For hotels, stay in Kurseong at the WBTDC Kurseong Tourism Property or Cochrane Place, or in Darjeeling at the WBTDC Darjeeling Tourism Property, Dekeling or the Windamere, and visit Mungpoo for half a day.
costs: Reserved car day trip from Darjeeling
Shared jeep seat, Darjeeling or Siliguri → Mungpoo
Free or a small fee, indicative
Tea and snacks in the bazaar
budget_tip: Do Mungpoo on the way to a Sittong homestay rather than as a separate day trip, so one car covers both and you save a full day's hire.
tips: Check Rabindra Bhavan's opening hours locally before you go; they can change and the museum may close on some days.
Do not photograph inside the museum unless the caretaker allows it.
Carry cash; there is no reliable ATM in Mungpoo.
Plan for early May if you want to see the Tagore birth anniversary programme at Rabindra Bhavan.
Avoid driving here from June to September if you can; landslides on the narrow roads are common in the monsoon.

experiences.title: Rabindra Bhavan, where Tagore stayed
experiences.cost: Free or a small fee, indicative
experiences.summary: Visit the house where Rabindranath Tagore stayed with Maitreyi Devi and her husband on four visits between 1938 and 1940. Now a small museum, it keeps his furniture, photographs, letters and reproductions of his paintings in a quiet setting among cinchona slopes.
body: Rabindra Bhavan is the bungalow of Dr Manmohan Sen, the quinine factory's chemist, and his wife Maitreyi Devi, who had known Tagore since she was a girl. The poet came to stay with them four times between 1938 and 1940, in poor health and in the last years of his life. He wrote, painted and talked here, and Maitreyi Devi later recorded their conversations in her book Mangpute Rabindranath.

The museum is small, and you can see it in under an hour. The rooms keep furniture that Tagore used, including a chair and desk, along with photographs of his visits, copies of letters and manuscripts, and reproductions of his paintings. Labels are mostly in Bengali and English. Caretakers often share stories of the poet's stays, and of the house's later years, when it was neglected and then restored as a memorial.

Check opening hours locally before you go, since they can change and the museum may close on some days. Photography inside may not be allowed. Keep your voice low; for many visitors from Bengal this is a place of real feeling. If you can, come on or around 25 Baishakh, Tagore's birth anniversary in early May, when the house fills with songs and recitations.

faqs.q: Why did Tagore visit Mungpoo
faqs.a: Tagore came to Mungpoo as the guest of Maitreyi Devi, whom he had known since her childhood, and her husband Dr Manmohan Sen, a chemist at the government quinine factory. He visited four times between 1938 and 1940, in the last years of his life, for rest and quiet. Their house is now the Rabindra Bhavan museum.

faqs.q: What is there to see at Rabindra Bhavan Mungpoo
faqs.a: The museum keeps furniture Tagore used, including a chair and desk, photographs of his visits, copies of letters and manuscripts and reproductions of his paintings. The rooms are small and the visit takes under an hour. Labels are in Bengali and English, and caretakers often share stories of the poet's stays.

faqs.q: What are the opening hours of Rabindra Bhavan Mungpoo
faqs.a: It is generally open during daytime hours, but timings and closing days change, and the museum may shut on some days or holidays. Ask your hotel, homestay or driver to confirm before you set out. A small entry fee may be charged. Check current status before you travel, especially if you are coming far for it.

experiences.title: Through the cinchona plantations
experiences.summary: Drive or walk the plantation roads around Mungpoo, where cinchona trees have been grown for quinine since the colonial era. See the slender trees on the slopes, the old factory buildings and staff quarters, and learn how a malaria cure shaped this corner of the hills.
body: Cinchona is a South American tree whose bark contains quinine, for long the main treatment for malaria. In the nineteenth century the British brought cinchona to India to cut the cost of importing quinine, and the government planted it in the Darjeeling hills, where Mungpoo became a centre of cultivation and processing. Today the plantations are run by the West Bengal government's cinchona directorate, which also manages estates at Latpanchar and elsewhere.

The trees are slim, with glossy leaves, and they grow in rows on the steep slopes around the village. Walk or drive slowly along the plantation roads and you will see staff quarters, the old factory area and workers tending the trees. The landscape looks different from tea country: taller, looser and greener, with patches of forest between the plantation blocks. Views open towards the Teesta valley on the clearer days.

Do not enter factory buildings or plantation blocks without permission; they are government property and not set up for visitors. A walk along the public roads is fine. Combine the drive with Rabindra Bhavan in the morning and continue to Sittong for lunch. In spring some plantation slopes flower, and in winter the air is clear for photographs. Leeches and slips make the monsoon a poor time to walk here.

faqs.q: What is cinchona and why is it grown in Mungpoo
faqs.a: Cinchona is a tree from South America whose bark contains quinine, long used to treat malaria. The British planted it in the Darjeeling hills in the nineteenth century to produce quinine in India, and Mungpoo became a centre of cultivation and processing. The plantations are still managed by the West Bengal government's cinchona directorate.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit the cinchona factory in Mungpoo
faqs.a: Factory buildings and plantation blocks are government property and are not normally open to tourists. You can see the plantations, staff quarters and old buildings from public roads on a drive or walk. If you have a research or special interest, you would need prior permission from the authorities. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Mungpoo a tea garden
faqs.a: No. Unlike most of the Darjeeling hills, Mungpoo's slopes are mainly planted with cinchona, the quinine tree, not tea. There are tea gardens nearby on the roads to Kurseong and Darjeeling. The difference is easy to see: cinchona trees are tall and slender, while tea bushes are clipped low into neat rows.

experiences.title: Tagore's birthday at Rabindra Bhavan
experiences.summary: Each year on 25 Baishakh, Tagore's birth anniversary in the Bengali calendar, Rabindra Bhavan in Mungpoo holds songs, recitations and gatherings in his memory. Local schools and visitors from Bengal take part, and the small museum fills with music.
body: Rabindranath Tagore was born on 7 May 1861, which in the Bengali calendar is 25 Baishakh. Bengalis everywhere mark the day as Rabindra Jayanti with his songs, Rabindra Sangeet, and readings of his poems. At Mungpoo, the house where he stayed with Maitreyi Devi becomes the centre of a small, local celebration, with schoolchildren, community groups and visitors gathering in and around Rabindra Bhavan.

Programmes vary from year to year but usually include songs, recitations, speeches and garlanding of the poet's portrait. The scale is modest and warm, very different from the large events in Kolkata or Santiniketan. Arrive in the morning to see the opening. Seating is limited, so be ready to stand. Dress modestly and keep phones on silent during performances.

Early May is a pleasant time in the hills, warm by day with afternoon showers, and it falls in the busy summer season, so book any stay well ahead. Ask locally for the exact date and programme, since the Gregorian date of 25 Baishakh shifts by a day and schedules depend on organisers. Combine the visit with a night in Sittong or Kurseong.

faqs.q: When is Tagore's birthday celebrated in Mungpoo
faqs.a: On 25 Baishakh in the Bengali calendar, which falls on 8 or 9 May in most years, when Rabindra Bhavan hosts songs, recitations and gatherings. The exact Gregorian date and programme vary, so ask locally or check with a Darjeeling agent. Arrive in the morning, as most events start early and space is limited.

faqs.q: Is the Rabindra Jayanti programme in Mungpoo open to tourists
faqs.a: Yes, visitors are generally welcome to watch the songs and recitations at Rabindra Bhavan. It is a local, community event, so be respectful: dress modestly, sit or stand where shown, keep phones silent and ask before photographing performers, especially children. There is usually no fee.

faqs.q: Where should I stay for Rabindra Jayanti in Mungpoo
faqs.a: Mungpoo has only a few small homestays and lodges, which fill quickly around the anniversary. Book early, or stay in nearby Sittong, Kurseong or Darjeeling and drive in for the morning. Early May is the hill summer season, so rooms everywhere cost more and sell out; book several weeks ahead.

experiences.title: Mungpoo, Sittong and Kurseong in one day
experiences.summary: A full-day loop from Darjeeling or Kurseong through the quiet lower hills: Tagore's house at Mungpoo, cinchona slopes, Sittong's orange orchards and back via Kurseong's tea gardens. Best in winter, when oranges hang on the trees and the skies are clear.
body: Leave Darjeeling by 8 am. Drive down through Ghum and on towards Mungpoo, reaching Rabindra Bhavan by mid-morning. Spend an hour at the museum, then drive slowly through the cinchona plantations, stopping for views over the Teesta valley. Tea and snacks in Mungpoo's small bazaar cost little. Ask your driver which road is in the best condition that day; the lower hill roads change with the weather.

From Mungpoo continue to Sittong, a short drive away, for lunch. Some homestays will cook a simple meal for day visitors if you call ahead. From November to January, walk the orange orchards after lunch and buy a basket of mandarins directly from a family. Outside the season, the village and its terraces are still worth a stroll. If you have time, add Latpanchar or Ahaldara, but that makes a long day.

Return via Kurseong, stopping at a tea estate or the Kurseong toy-train station on the way, and reach Darjeeling by evening. A reserved car for the loop costs about ₹3,500–5,000, indicative 2026, depending on stops. It is cheaper to split between four people. If you can, break the loop with a night in Sittong instead; it makes the day far less rushed.

faqs.q: Can I visit Mungpoo and Sittong in one day
faqs.a: Yes. They are close together, so a full day from Darjeeling or Kurseong can cover Rabindra Bhavan at Mungpoo, the cinchona slopes and Sittong's orchards. A reserved car costs about ₹3,500–5,000, indicative 2026. Leave by 8 am, call a Sittong homestay ahead for lunch, and return via Kurseong by evening.

faqs.q: How far is Mungpoo from Darjeeling
faqs.a: Mungpoo is about 35 km from Darjeeling, typically 1.5–2 hours by road depending on route and conditions. A reserved car for a day trip costs about ₹2,500–3,500, indicative 2026. A few shared jeeps run, but timings are limited. The roads are narrow and winding, so allow extra time after rain.

faqs.q: Is the Mungpoo–Sittong loop good in the monsoon
faqs.a: Not really. From June to September, the narrow roads in these lower hills often suffer landslides and slips, views are hidden in cloud and leeches make walking unpleasant. If you must go, travel by daylight with a local driver, keep the plan flexible and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where is Mungpoo
faqs.a: Mungpoo is a small plantation settlement in the Kurseong subdivision of Darjeeling district, at about 1,150 m, above the Teesta valley. It is roughly 35 km from Darjeeling, close to Sittong, and about 55–60 km from Siliguri. It is known for the government cinchona plantations and for Rabindra Bhavan, where Tagore stayed.

faqs.q: Is Mungpoo worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, if you are interested in Tagore, Bengali literature or plantation history, or if you want a quiet half day off the usual Darjeeling circuit. There is not much else, so most people spend one to three hours here and combine it with Sittong or Kurseong. Travellers looking for big views or shopping may find it too quiet.

faqs.q: How many times did Tagore visit Mungpoo
faqs.a: Rabindranath Tagore visited Mungpoo four times between 1938 and 1940, staying with Maitreyi Devi and her husband Dr Manmohan Sen. These were the last years of his life; he died in August 1941. Maitreyi Devi recorded his visits in her Bengali book Mangpute Rabindranath, and the house is now Rabindra Bhavan.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Mungpoo
faqs.a: October to April is best, with dry roads and clear views, and winter adds Sittong's orange season nearby. Early May brings Tagore's birth anniversary programme at Rabindra Bhavan. Avoid June to September, when landslides often affect the narrow roads. Check current status before you travel in wet months.

faqs.q: How do I reach Mungpoo from Siliguri
faqs.a: Take a reserved car from Siliguri, NJP or Bagdogra, about ₹3,000–4,500 and 2–2.5 hours, indicative 2026. A few shared jeeps run from Siliguri, usually once or twice a day, ₹100–200 a seat. Routes depend on road conditions, so let your driver choose and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in Mungpoo
faqs.a: Yes, but choices are few: a handful of small homestays and simple lodges, usually ₹1,200–2,500 per person per day with meals, indicative 2026. Many travellers prefer Sittong, which is close and has more homestays, or Kurseong for hotels. Book ahead around Tagore's birth anniversary in early May.

faqs.q: Who was Maitreyi Devi
faqs.a: Maitreyi Devi was a Bengali writer and poet, born in 1914, daughter of the philosopher Surendranath Dasgupta and a protégée of Rabindranath Tagore. She hosted Tagore at her home in Mungpoo and wrote about it in Mangpute Rabindranath. Her novel Na Hanyate, a reply to Mircea Eliade's Bengal Nights, won the Sahitya Akademi Award.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Rabindra Bhavan Mungpoo
faqs.a: Entry is free or a small fee, and charges may apply for cameras. Opening days and hours can change, and the museum may close on some days. Confirm locally before you travel, especially if Mungpoo is the main purpose of your trip. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What else can I see near Mungpoo
faqs.a: Sittong's orange orchards and homestays are a short drive away. Latpanchar, inside Mahananda Wildlife Sanctuary, is known for hornbills and has its own cinchona plantation, and nearby Ahaldara viewpoint looks over the Teesta valley. Kurseong's tea gardens and toy-train station are about an hour away, and Darjeeling about 1.5–2 hours.
